2. The parties shall henceforth be referred as they were arrayed before the Trial Court in O.S.1232/2006.
The appellant herein was the plaintiff while the respondents No.2 and 3 were the defendants No.1 and 2 in O.S.No.1232/2006.

The respondent No.1 herein was not a party in the suit but he filed R.A.No.5030/2016 challenging the judgment and decree in O.S. No.1232/2006 and hence he would henceforth be referred to as "non-party defendant".

3. The suit in O.S.No.1232/2006 was filed for declaration that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit property and since it was allowed to remain in possession for over 25 years, it had acquired a statutory right to call upon the defendants to execute a deed of absolute sale.
A declaration was also sought that the threat of the defendants to resume possession of a portion of the property was not justified.
A declaration was also sought that the plaintiff had substantially complied with all the terms and conditions of the lease cum sale deed and the defendants were bound to execute a sale deed.

A further declaration was sought to declare that the proceedings initiated by the defendants on M/S. Sri. Ramachandra vs Sri. D. Muniyappa on 10 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137070430/
2 07.04.2005 and thereafter, were void and unenforceable.

sentences.text: The plaintiff sought for consequential relief of injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering or dispossessing it from suit schedule property.
4. The plaintiff claimed that the State Government had acquired land at Bommasandra, Attibele Hobli, for formation of an industrial area by the defendant No.1.
Consequently, defendant No.1 invited applications for allotment of industrial plots.

The plaintiff also applied for allotment of an industrial plot, consequent to which, an industrial plot bearing No.253 measuring 18,205 sq.mtrs.
was allotted and possession certificate dated 30.04.1982 was handed over and it was placed in possession.

The plaintiff claimed that it constructed a building to house an industrial unit to manufacture PVC leather and foam cloth and claimed that the entire property was utilised for the purposes of industrial activity.
The open space was used for ancillary purposes of the unit such as, to store steam coal, cinder coal ash, solvent and other materials.
The plaintiff claimed that the industrial plot was conveyed under a lease cum sale agreement, which was to be in force for a period of 11 years from 21.10.1981.
The plaintiff claimed that it had complied with all the terms and conditions of the lease cum sale agreement dated 17.06.1982 and it had paid the entire amount under the lease cum sale agreement.
It further claimed that a sum of Rs.3,00,000/- was demanded as a final installment, which too was paid.
After completion of 11 years as on 20.10.1992, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 were required to execute a deed of absolute sale in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property.
Though a request was made, defendants, failed to execute a deed of absolute sale.
Whenever requests were made by the plaintiff, to conclude the transaction, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not heed to the requests.
Therefore, the plaintiff claimed that it had perfected its right, title and interest and ownership over the plot.

However, the defendant No.2 addressed a letter dated 07.04.2005 and invoked Clause - 4 of lease cum sale agreement and stated that the lease would be terminated and the possession of the land would be resumed for violation of terms and conditions of lease cum sale agreement.
The plaintiff replied to the notice on 23.06.2005 and also made the payment as demanded by the defendant No.2.
Therefore, the plaintiff filed O.S.No.1232/2006 for the aforesaid reliefs.
5. The suit was contested by the defendant No.1 on the ground that it was obligated to execute a sale deed only after compliance of terms of lease and not on mere expiry of lease period.
It contended that the plaintiff did not establish the unit as claimed by it, but had not utilized a large space.
It contended that the notice issued by it on 07.04.2005 was in accordance with terms and conditions of lease cum sale agreement.
It claimed that the plaintiff did not get any right much less, a title by adverse possession, but in view of the lease cum sale agreement, could at the most be a tenant by holding over.

It claimed that since the reply of the plaintiff was not accepted, the lease cum sale agreement was terminated on 13.09.2005 in accordance with the terms contained therein, as the plaintiff failed to utilise the allotted land.

6. Based on these contentions the Trial Court framed the following issues:
"1. Whether the plaintiff proves that it has paid the entire amount and there are no dues in any manner whatsoever to the defendants in respect of lease- cum-sale of suit property?

Following the above, the non-party defendant filed R.A.No.5030/2016 challenging the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006.

The non-party defendant contended that his land bearing Sy.No.211 measuring 34 guntas situated at Bommasandra village, Attibele Hobli, Anekal taluk was part and parcel of the property involved in O.S.No.1232/2006.
He contended that his grand father purchased Sy.No.211 in terms of a sale deed 21.11.1925.
After his death, the father of the non-party defendant inherited it and such inheritance was recorded in the revenue records.
He claimed that this land was forfeited to the State Government for non-payment of land revenue.
The non-party defendant after coming to know of such forfeiture, filed an application under Section 163 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 for restoration of the land.
The Tahsildar passed an order dated 04.07.2014 and restored the names of the non-party defendant in Column No.11 of RTC of Sy.No.211 after he paid the entire arrears of the land revenue.

13. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree, the plaintiff has filed this Miscellaneous Second Appeal.

14. This appeal was admitted to consider the following substantial questions of law:
1.

Whether the lower appellate court was justified in entertaining the appeal filed by a person who was not party to the suit, when original defendant KIADB has accepted the judgment and decree passed by the court below, without challenging the same?

2. Whether the 1st respondent in the court below, appellant herein is justified in pursuing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court against KIADB instead of establishing his right by filing a suit independently?
3. Whether the lower appellate court was justified in remanding the matter back to the trial court at the instance of third party to original suit?

15. The learned counsel for the plaintiff contended as follows:
i) that the First Appellate Court failed to note that the land in Sy.No.211 measuring 32 guntas of Bommasandra village was already acquired by defendant No.2 in terms of a preliminary notification dated 28.02.1981 followed by a final notification and the possession of the property was taken and an award was passed in the year 1987. That the defendant No.1 had already formed an industrial area comprising several plots.

That in view of the threat of resumption, the plaintiff was forced to file O.S.No.1232/2006 which was ultimately decreed, as the Court found that the plaintiff had complied with all its obligation under the lease cum sale agreement;

iv) He further contended that since the defendant No.1 failed to execute the sale deed,
despite the judgment and decree in O.S.No.1232/2006, an execution petition in M/S. Sri. Ramachandra vs Sri. D. Muniyappa on 10 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137070430/

He contended that the non-party defendant was claiming title to the land bearing Sy.No.211, which was already acquired by the State Government for the defendant No.1 in the name of Siddappa S/o. Dodda Muniga and compensation was paid to him;
v)
He contended that the non-party defendant had also challenged the acquisition in W.P.No.47352/2014 and that the writ petition was dismissed as withdrawn.

Therefore, he contends that the challenge to the acquisition is rejected and hence, the non-party defendant has no subsisting right, title or interest to challenge the allotment of plot to the plaintiff;
vi) that the non-party defendant has filed a suit in O.S.No.546/2018 against the State Government and KIADB and his cousins for a declaration of his title in respect of the suit property and to declare that the award dated 23-10-1986 passed in favour of the father of the defendant Nos.3 and 4 in respect of the suit property is null and void and not binding on him.

He therefore contended that the question whether the property of the non-party defendant was acquired or not and whether he was bound by the allotment of industrial plot or not, were all questions which were outside the scope of suit and therefore, the First Appellate Court should not have entertained the appeal filed by the non-party defendant.
Therefore, he contends that the First Appellate Court should not have granted leave to challenge the judgment decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006.

He further contended that the non- party defendant had no locus standi to challenge the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006 as he was not an applicant seeking an industrial plot and no site was allotted to him;

i) that the lease cum sale agreement in favour of the plaintiff was terminated by defendant No.1 on 13.09.2005 due to non-utilisation of the land allotted to the plaintiff from 1982 till 2005.

17. The learned counsel for the defendant Nos.1 and 2 had filed a written synopsis:

This Court in terms of the order dated 27.02.2023, appointed a Commissioner to verify whether the industrial plot allotted to the plaintiff was vacant or whether a factory was constructed by the plaintiff over it.

The Commissioner appointed by the Court has submitted a report stating that he found a factory constructed in the plot No.253 formed in Sy.Nos.209, 210 and 212, while, a portion of the land in Sy.No.210 was left vacant.

He found that on the front portion of the land bearing Sy.No.211 there were four hotels and three shops, and a part of the property was utilised for a farm house, where the southern side of the said property was left vacant.
He also noticed that a wall was laid between Sy.Nos.210 and 211.
The Commissioner was therefore of the opinion that an industry was functioning in the front portion of Sy.No.210, while the rear portion was vacant.
While, a portion of Sy.No.211 was used for a farm house and the remaining was left vacant.

19. The learned counsel for KIADB has placed on record an order of termination of lease whereby,
the allotment of plot No.253 was terminated and 7500 sq.mtrs., of the plot area was resumed on 14.10.2005.
20.

This apart, the non-party defendant has furnished a copy of the agreement of sale dated 07.12.2015 which indicated that he had agreed to sell 34 guntas of land in Sy.No.211 in favour of Mr.
K.P. Abdulla and others, which culminated in a sale deed dated 07.08.2021 in favour of Mr.

another sale deed dated 12.04.2023 in favour of Mr. Muhammed Arafath Pallipath and a sale deed dated 21.11.2023 in favour of Mr. Ibrahim.
Therefore, the non-party defendant does not have any subsisting interest in the property.

21. I have considered the submissions made by the learned counsel for the plaintiff, learned counsel for the non- party defendant, and learned counsel for defendant Nos.1 and 2.
22.
A perusal of the reliefs sought in O.S.No.1232/2006 shows that it was essentially related to allotment of an industrial plot bearing No.253 by the defendant Nos.1 and 2 to the plaintiff.
The defendant Nos.1 and 2 claimed that the plaintiff had not utilised 7500 sq.mtrs., of the allotted land and thereby had terminated the lease on 13.09.2005.
The plaintiff claimed that it had implemented the project on a portion of allotted land and was using the remaining space for storage.

It claimed that since it had done everything that was expected of it, and as it was allowed to remain in possession of the allotted plot for over 25 years, it was entitled to call upon the defendant Nos.1 and 2 to conclude the allotment.
The defendant Nos.1 and 2 filed their written statement alleging that the allotment was cancelled on 13.09.2005 and therefore, the suit before the Civil Court was not maintainable.

However, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 neither cross-examined the plaintiff in O.S.No.1232/2006 nor did they enter the witness box to support their contentions that the lease cum sale agreement was terminated on 13.09.2005 and possession of the land was taken over.

It is seen that decree in O.S.No.1232/2006 was put in execution in E.P.No.17/2009 and a sale deed dated 11.06.2010 was executed by the Court conveying plot No.253 to the plaintiff formed in Sy.Nos.209 to 212.
Therefore, if the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were aggrieved by the said judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006, they were bound to challenge it by filing an appeal.

However,
they failed to do so.

In the meanwhile, the non-party defendant filed R.A.No.5030/2016 contending that he was the owner of the land bearing Sy.No.211 measuring 34 guntas and that the same was forfeited by the State Government for non-payment of arrears of land revenue.

He claimed that he filed an appeal before the Tahsildar who cancelled the forfeiture of the land upon payment of arrears M/S. Sri. Ramachandra vs Sri. D. Muniyappa on 10 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137070430/
10 of land revenue

He contended that an appeal was preferred by him under Section 136 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 who passed an order restoring the name of the non-party defendant in Column No.9 of the RTC and the right of KIABD in column No.11.
It is undisputed that the land in Sy.No.211 was acquired by the defendant No.2 for the purpose of acquisition.
The non-party defendant challenged the acquisition of Sy.No.211 in W.P.No.47352/2014 and which is now dismissed as withdrawn.
Therefore, the non-party defendant in R.A.No.5030/20156 was not in any way interested or aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006.

None the less,
he challenged the judgment and decree in O.S.No.1232/2006 before this Court in W.P.10714/2016,
which was dismissed but on his request, liberty was reserved to him to challenge the Judgment and Decree in O.S.No.1232/2006 before the appropriate Court.

However, he took advantage of the liberty so granted and challenged the judgment and decree passed therein in R.A.No.5030/2016.
24.

It is now well settled that an appeal is a substantial right created under a statute in favour of a person who is aggrieved by any order or act and no Court can confer any such right to file an appeal on a person who has no locus standi.

Consequently, the non-party defendant was bound to establish his locus standi to challenge the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006, not withstanding the liberty granted to him by this Court in W.P.No.10714/2016.
The non-party defendant challenged the acquisition of Sy.No.211, but later withdrew it, which established beyond doubt that he had consented to the acquisition of land bearing Sy.No.211.

This apart, the non-party defendant had filed O.S.No.546/2018 for a declaration of his title in respect of the land in Sy.No.211 and for a declaration that the award dated 23-10-1986 passed in the name of Siddappa was null and void and not binding upon him.
This also established beyond doubt that the non-party defendant had accepted the acquisition of Sy.No.211 of Bommasandra village, by the State government under the provisions of the KIADB Act.
Thus, his locus standi to contest the decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006 is very doubtful.

Therefore, strictly speaking, the non-party defendant was not really interested in the suit and he was prima facie not a proper and necessary party for the adjudication of the suit in O.S.No.1232/2006.
If it affected the interest of the non-party defendant in any manner, then it was for him to file an appropriate suit to protect his interest in the land bearing Sy.No.211.

The contention that 7500 sq.mtrs., of the land was resumed by KIADB after canceling the allotment in favour of the plaintiff, did not arm the non-party defendant with any cause of action to challenge the judgment and decree passed in the suit.
If any person was aggrieved by the judgment and decree in O.S.No.1232/2006 it was only KIADB and its officers and it was for them to challenge the judgment and decree passed therein.

25. The defendant Nos.2 and 3 who did not contest the suit have obliquely filed an application before this Court to uphold the order of remand on the ground that a specific bar is contained in Sections 25 and 45 of the KIADB Act which are extracted below:

"25. Application of [Karnataka Act 32 of 1974] to Board premises: (1) The State Government, may by notification provide from such date as may be specified in such notification that the [Karnataka Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1974] shall apply to premises belonging to, vesting in, or leased by,

11 provisions of sub-section (2).

(a) the State Government may appoint any officer whether under the Government or the Board, as it thinks fit, to be the competent officer for the purposes of the aforesaid Act;

26.
A perusal of both the provisions do not indicate how the suit in O.S.No.1232/2006 was not maintainable.

This apart, the issue in O.S.1232/2006 related to the enforceability of the lease cum sale agreement and the corresponding obligation on the part of the defendant Nos.1 and 2 to conclude the allotment of land by executing a deed of absolute sale.
It is not the case of the defendants that even prior to the filing of the suit in O.S.1232/2006, the lease cum sale agreement was cancelled and the possession of 7500 sq.mtrs., was resumed.
If the same was done subsequent to the filing of the suit, it did not affect the suit in any manner and the Court could grant the reliefs.
This apart, there is nothing in the KIADB Act which ousts the jurisdiction of the Civil Court in matters relating to the enforcement of the lease cum sale.

Therefore, the contention of the learned counsel for the defendant Nos.1 and 2 that the judgment of the First Appellate Court in R.A.5030/2016 should be upheld, is liable to be rejected and is accordingly rejected.
The application filed by the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in I.A.No.1/2021 is therefore rejected.
27. It is relevant to note that the suit in O.S.No.1720/2005 was filed on 03.08.2005 and later was transferred to the Court at Anekal and renumbered as O.S.No.1232/2006.
The defendant No.2 claimed that plot allotted to the plaintiff was cancelled on 13.09.2005 which was after the suit was filed in O.S.No.1720/2005.
Hence, the issue before the Court was whether the cancellation was in accordance with the lease cum sale agreement.

Since the defendant Nos.2 and 3 did not contest the suit, the Court was constrained to hold that the proceedings to terminate the lease cum sale agreement were improper and not in accordance with the terms and conditions of lease cum sale agreement and consequently, directed the defendant Nos.2 and 3 to execute the sale conveying the industrial plot to plaintiff.
This therefore, did not affect the non-party defendant as his property was also acquired and used up for formation of industrial layout.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Therefore, the non-party defendant in R.A.No.5030/20156 was not in any way interested or aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006.
It is now well settled that an appeal is a substantial right created under a statute in favour of a person who is aggrieved by any order or act and no Court can confer any such right to file an appeal on a person who has no locus standi.
Consequently, the non-party defendant was bound to establish his locus standi to challenge the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006, not withstanding the liberty granted to him by this Court in W.P.No.10714/2016.
If the same was done subsequent to the filing of the suit, it did not affect the suit in any manner and the Court could grant the reliefs.
This apart, there is nothing in the KIADB Act which ousts the jurisdiction of the Civil Court in matters relating to the enforcement of the lease cum sale.
Since the defendant Nos.2 and 3 did not contest the suit, the Court was constrained to hold that the proceedings to terminate the lease cum sale agreement were improper and not in accordance with the terms and conditions of lease cum sale agreement and consequently, directed the defendant Nos.2 and 3 to execute the sale conveying the industrial plot to plaintiff.
This therefore, did not affect the non-party defendant as his property was also acquired and used up for formation of industrial layout.
That the non-party defendant who had admitted  the acquisition of land in Sy.No.211 of  Bommasandra village and who was not an applicant for allotment of industrial plot could not have challenged the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court against KIADB.
29. Under the circumstance, First Appellate Court committed an error of sorts in entertaining the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree passed in O.S.No.1232/2006.
In view of the findings recorded above,
there is no doubt that the First Appellate Court could not have allowed the appeal and remitted the case to the Trial Court for a de-novo trial and disposal.
